questions.prompt: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write a news report to your campus newspaper on a visit to a local farm organized by your Student Union. You should write at least 120 words but no more than 180 words.
questions.correctAnswer:
A Visit That Brought Farming Closer

Last Saturday, the Student Union organized a visit to a local farm, giving students an opportunity to understand where their food comes from. Thirty volunteers joined the activity and received a warm welcome from the farmers.

The visit began with a short introduction to seasonal crops. Students then helped plant vegetables and learned how to water young plants without wasting resources. A farmer explained that successful farming requires patience as well as practical knowledge. During the discussion, participants asked questions about food safety and the difficulties faced by small farms.

The activity ended with students sharing their observations. Many said that they would appreciate every meal more and reduce food waste. The Student Union plans to organize similar visits in the future, helping students connect classroom knowledge with everyday life.

questions.hint: 用新闻体交代谁组织、何时何地、参观活动与意义。
questions.explanation:
以下为按题意独立写成的参考范文，作文没有唯一答案。标题后用过去时报道农场参观；种植体验和节约粮食体现活动价值。日期、人数及细节是示范设定，不表示真实新闻。

写作步骤：第一段用组织者、时间、地点、参与者回答新闻导语的问题；第二段按参观顺序写农作物介绍、种植体验及交流；第三段写参与者感想和后续计划。organized a visit to是组织参观，reduce food waste是减少食物浪费。开头和活动过程用过去时，未来计划可用plans to。自查报道是否真的发生在农场，别改成赞美农业的重要性；示范人数与日期可换成自己的合理设定。

练习方法：先用提示列三段提纲，在30分钟内独立写作，再按下方标准逐项打分；把失分最多的一段重写。参考范文约136词（缩写、连字符词按一词，含标题或书信称呼落款），满足120–180词要求；评分用于练习自检，不代表官方阅卷分数。
rubric: 练习自评总分15分：题目覆盖0–6＋结构0–4＋语言0–5，先独立写完再对照；观点不同于范文也可得满分，只要有合理支持。
题目覆盖0–6分：该题检查——用新闻体交代谁组织、何时何地、参观活动与意义。。6分=任务完整且有具体理由/活动/例证；4–5分=切题但细节偏薄；2–3分=遗漏主要任务；0–1分=基本离题。
结构0–4分：4分=开头明确任务、主体按逻辑展开、结尾回扣，段间自然；3分=顺序清楚但局部衔接生硬；1–2分=跳跃或机械罗列；0分=内容难以组织理解。
语言0–5分：5分=语法和用词基本准确、句型有变化；3–4分=少量错误但不影响理解；1–2分=反复出现时态、主谓一致或搭配错误并影响阅读；0分=多数句子不能理解。
格式与修订：按原题保持120–180词；新闻/书信/提案用对应体裁，明确要求的首句逐字保留。若超限、少写任务或缺必要格式，先修改再评分，不把字数达标当作内容满分。

questions.prompt: An extended lifespan in the future will allow people to have more careers than now.
questions.passage:
How Work Will Change When Most of Us Live to 100

A) Today in the United States there are 72,000 centenarians(百岁老人). Worldwide, probably 450,000. If current trends continue, then by 2050 there will be more than a million in the US alone. According to the work of Professor James Vaupel and his co-researchers, 50% of babies born in the US in 2007 have a life expectancy of 104 or more. Broadly the same holds for the UK, Germany, France, Italy and Canada, and for Japan 50% of 2007 babies can expect to live to 107.

questions.prompt: How might people often feel when they were misnamed?
questions.passage:
If you were like most children, you probably got upset when your mother called you by a sibling's(兄弟姐妹的) name. How could she not know you? Did it mean she loved you less?

Probably not. According to the first research to tackle this topic head-on, misnaming the most familiar people in our life is a common cognitive(认知的) error that has to do with how our memories classify and store familiar names.

The study, published online in April in the journal Memory and Cognition, found that the "wrong" name is not random but is invariably fished out from the same relationship pond: children, siblings, friends. The study did not examine the possibility of deep psychological significance to the mistake, says psychologist David Rubin, "but it does tell us who's in and who's out of the group."

The study also found that within that group, misnamings occurred where the names shared initial or internal sounds, like Jimmy and Joanie or John and Bob. Physical resemblance between people was not a factor. Nor was gender.

The researchers conducted five separate surveys of more than 1,700 people. Some of the surveys included only college students; others were done with a mixed-age population. Some asked subjects about incidents where someone close to them—family or friend—had called them by another person's name. The other surveys asked about times when subjects had themselves called someone close to them by the wrong name. All the surveys found that people mixed up names within relationship groups such as grandchildren, friends and siblings but hardly ever crossed these boundaries.

In general, the study found that undergraduates were almost as likely as old people to make this mistake and men as likely as women. Older people and women made the mistake slightly more often, but that may be because grandparents have more grandchildren to mix up than parents have children. Also, mothers may call on their children more often than fathers, given traditional gender norms. There was no evidence that errors occurred more when the misnamer was frustrated, tired or angry.

灯笼起源于东汉，最初主要用于照明。在唐代，人们用红灯笼来庆祝安定的生活。从那时起，灯笼在中国的许多地方流行起来。灯笼通常用色彩鲜艳的薄纸制作，形状和尺寸各异。在中国传统文化中，红灯笼象征生活美满和生意兴隆，通常在春节、元宵节和国庆等节日期间悬挂。如今，世界上许多其他地方也能看到红灯笼。
questions.correctAnswer: Lanterns originated in the Eastern Han Dynasty and were first used mainly for lighting. During the Tang Dynasty, people celebrated a peaceful life with red lanterns. Since then, lanterns have become popular in many parts of China. Usually made of brightly colored thin paper, they come in various shapes and sizes. In traditional Chinese culture, red lanterns symbolize a happy life and a flourishing business. They are commonly hung during festivals such as the Spring Festival, the Lantern Festival and National Day. Today, red lanterns can also be seen in many other places around the world.
